H1.text: A mushroom on the lawn. A green speck swimming in pond water. The bacteria that set your curd.

H2.text: Plant or animal? None of them fits cleanly.

H3.text: Diya found a mushroom in the college garden after the rain. It grows from the soil and never moves, just like a plant.

H4.text: Yet biologists say a mushroom is not a plant. Why?

H5.text: By the end, you will know the seven questions scientists ask before they place a living thing, and why the old two kingdom system broke.

B1.text: People have sorted living things for a very long time.

B2.text: Aristotle made the first scientific try. He sorted plants by their simple form into trees, shrubs and herbs.

B3.text: He split animals into two groups: those with red blood, and those without.

B4.text: Much later, Linnaeus used just two kingdoms. Plantae for plants, and Animalia for animals.

S1.text: Let's run the two kingdom sort, and watch it break.

S2.text: A mango tree goes into Plantae. A cat goes into Animalia. Easy.

S3.text: A mushroom does not move, so it was put in Plantae. But it has no chlorophyll, and cannot make its own food.

S4.text: A bacterium went into Plantae too. But its cell has no nucleus at all.

S5.text: And Euglena is green like a plant, but swims like an animal. It fits neither box.

S6.text: So two boxes mixed up three big differences.

S7.text: First, cells with a true nucleus, and cells without one.

S8.text: Second, living things made of one cell, and those made of many.

S9.text: Third, green algae that make food, and fungi that cannot. Both were called plants.

Z1.text: Now let's settle the mushroom question. Zoom in, one level at a time.

Z2.text: Here is the mushroom. A cap, gills under the cap, and a stalk.

Z3.text: Zoom in. The whole mushroom is made of thin threads called hyphae, packed tightly together. No leaves, no true roots.

Z4.text: Zoom again. One hypha is a tube of cells, with nuclei and cross walls. But look, there are no chloroplasts. It cannot make food from sunlight.

Z5.text: Zoom into the wall. A plant cell wall is made of cellulose. A mushroom's wall is made of chitin, the same tough material found in an insect's outer skeleton.

C1.text: So what do biologists check? Seven things. Each one is a test.

C2.text: One. Cell type. Is it a simple prokaryotic cell, or a eukaryotic cell with parts wrapped in membranes?

C3.text: Two. Cell wall. Is there a wall, and what is it made of?

C4.text: Three. Nuclear membrane. Is the DNA kept inside a membrane, or lying loose in the cell?

C5.text: Four. Body organisation. One cell, loose threads, or tissues and organs?

C6.text: Five. Mode of nutrition. Does it make its own food? That is autotrophic. Or does it take food from others? That is heterotrophic.

C7.text: Six. Reproduction. How does it make more of itself? Spores, seeds, or simple splitting?

C8.text: Seven. Phylogenetic relationships. Which groups share a common ancestor? Phylogeny means the family history of living things.

P1.text: The first test splits all of life in two. Let's compare.

P2.text: A prokaryotic cell, like the bacterium in curd, is small and simple. Its DNA lies loose. There is no nuclear membrane.

P3.text: A eukaryotic cell, like a yeast cell, keeps its DNA inside a nucleus, wrapped in a nuclear membrane, and has other parts wrapped in membranes too.

P4.text: Your turn. Cyanobacteria are green and make their own food. Is their cell prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Pause and decide.

P5.text: Prokaryotic! Cyanobacteria are bacteria. Being green does not give a cell a nucleus.

T1.text: Remember this. Classify by the cell and the food, not by the looks.

W1.text: Now, a worked example. Let's sort five living things with just four questions.

W2.text: Question one. Is there a nuclear membrane? The curd bacterium says no. It drops into its own box.

W3.text: Question two. Is it a single cell? Euglena says yes. A box for one celled eukaryotes.

W4.text: Question three. Does it make its own food? The mango tree says yes.

W5.text: Question four. Is there a chitin wall? The mushroom says yes. The cat has no cell wall at all.

W6.text: Five living things, five boxes, not two.

X2.text: Many students think, it has a cell wall, so it must be a plant.

X3.text: But bacteria and fungi have walls too. What the wall is made of matters, and plants also make their own food.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As statements on why the two kingdom system failed, or on which features are used to classify.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Read the four statements. Which ones are correct? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Statements two and three.

A2.text: One is wrong. A mushroom's wall is made of chitin, not cellulose.

A3.text: Four is wrong. Phylogeny means shared ancestry, not body size.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is a mushroom not a plant?

Y3.text: Two. Which three differences did the two kingdom system miss?

Y4.text: Three. What is the difference between autotrophic and heterotrophic?

N1.text: Next time: one scientist drew five boxes instead of two. What goes into each? We find out in five kingdom classification.
